title: Ashtpadi 13, salok: the holy

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 12, mithat neevee, and your line: humility first. Did you manage a plain sorry, with nothing after it? Today a new ashtpadi, the thirteenth, and a new stretch of Sukhmani. Day four hundred eighty-six.

Who's the best person you actually know? Not the most famous, not the most impressive. The best. Maybe a neighbor who shovels the whole block's sidewalks and never mentions it. An aunt who remembers every birthday. A nurse who stayed after her shift. Somebody probably came to mind. Now the harder question: have you ever told them? Applause is easy to give a stranger on a stage. It's oddly hard to give the neighbor with the shovel. The salok of the thirteenth ashtpadi starts right there: with the good ones, and what it means to stand near them.
screen: `THE BEST PERSON YOU KNOW.` → `NOT FAMOUS. GOOD.` → `HAVE YOU EVER TOLD THEM?`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines, and they pull in opposite directions. The first, in paraphrase: whoever takes shelter with the saints is carried across. The second: whoever slanders the saints, Nanak, is born again and again. Today we stay with the first line; tomorrow the ashtpadi turns to the second, and spends a long time there. First, the word. Sant. It's usually translated saint, but be careful. In the Guru Granth Sahib, sant isn't a rank anyone hands out. It describes a person whose life is soaked in remembering God: honest, humble, kind, steady. Sukhmani has already described such people in earlier ashtpadis, the holy company and the God-conscious one. They might run a shop. They might be your grandmother. Next, the verb: saran. Shelter, refuge, the way you'd step under an awning when it rains. The salok isn't asking you to worship good people. It's saying that nearness to them changes you. Sikhs call it sangat, the company, and Sikh worship gathers around it: praying together, singing together, eating together in the langar. Goodness, in this picture, is catching. You stand near it long enough and some of it rubs off, the way a cloth takes on the scent of the flowers it's wrapped around. Then the second line hangs over the first like a cloud: if nearness lifts you, contempt for the good drags you down. That's tomorrow. Today's job is simpler. Notice the good people. Honor them.
screen: `TWO LINES, OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS.` · `SANT: A LIFE SOAKED IN THE NAME.` · `SARAN: SHELTER UNDER AN AWNING.` · `GOODNESS IS CATCHING.` · then, large: `HONOR THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a good person. Bring one to mind, someone whose goodness is quiet. See their face. Remember one specific thing they did, a small one is best. Hold it there and let yourself be grateful that people like this exist. Then, if you like, picture telling them so, in one plain sentence. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Sant, a holy person. Soaked in remembering God; shelter near such people, the salok says, carries you across.
Your line: honor the good. Today, tell one good person, out loud or in a message, one specific thing you admire about them. Day four hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib reach the thirteenth ashtpadi's salok on the sant, and Sikh life places great weight on sangat, the company of the good, in shared prayer, singing and the langar.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sant, a holy person; in the Guru Granth Sahib, one whose life is soaked in the Name.

trapdoor: what you thought: saints are a special class of officially holy people.
what it means: a sant is any person living close to God, and nearness to such people changes you.
what a scholar hears: in the Guru Granth Sahib, sant and saadh describe a quality of life rather than a rank, and the salok's second line opens a long run of stanzas on slander.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 13, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279)

notes: Salok of ashtpadi 13 paraphrased: sant saran jo jan parai so jan udharanhaar; sant kee nindaa Nanakaa bahur bahur avtaar. Confirm Ang 279.
Description of sant as a quality of life rather than a formal status: confirm the framing Keepers prefer; some Sikh usage today also uses sant as a title for preachers.
Flower-scent image is the writer's, not quoted from Gurbani.
